html:
An English, later British, trading company founded in London in 1600 that grew from buying cloth and spices into the ruler of most of India. It was dissolved in 1874.

Queen Elizabeth I gave it a monopoly of English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope on the last day of 1600. Shareholders put up money for voyages and shared the profits, an early form of joint-stock company. At first it sought spices in Indonesia, but the stronger Dutch East India Company pushed it out. So it turned to India, where it set up trading posts:

  • Surat in 1613,
  • Madras in 1639,
  • Bombay in 1668,
  • Calcutta in 1690.

For a century it mostly traded, above all in Indian cotton cloth, the calicoes that became a craze in Europe. As the Mughal Empire broke up, the Company armed itself, hired Indian soldiers and fought the French. Its victory at the Battle of Plassey in 1757 made it master of Bengal, and in 1765 it won the right to collect Bengal's taxes. Its rule in Bengal was soon followed by the famine of 1770.

Over the next eighty years the Company's armies, by then larger than the British army, defeated Mysore under Tipu Sultan, the Marathas and the Sikhs. It paid for Chinese tea with Indian opium, which led to the Opium War. Parliament gradually took control of it and ended its trade monopolies in 1813 and 1833. After the rebellion of 1857, the British Crown took over its territories, and the Company was wound up in 1874.
sum: An English, later British, trading company founded in London in 1600 that grew from buying cloth and spices into the ruler of most of India. It was dissolved in 1874.
